title: Klezmer Sorrow and Joy: “Doyna & Terkisher Tanz”—Prelude and Fugue No.9, Book II
content_blocks: You may have noticed that I’ve referenced New York City in some of my previous Blog Posts (“Funk,” June 29, and “The Skeptic,” July 2). I was born and raised in New York, a city I knew to be the center of world Jewish culture: humor…the 2nd Avenue Deli…but music? The little I knew of Jewish music, aside from synagogue music, was the cheesy, often clichéed wedding music of Hava Nagila. That changed years later, when I heard Klezmerata Fiorentina: music of great sorrow and joy, conveying centuries of pain and pleasure. Some buried memory came to the surface, as if I had known this side of Klezmer music all along. Well, I had known it all along: Klezmer—from the Hebrew for musical instruments—is just the secular side of the liturgical music that I had grown up with…I just hadn’t realized it.

A doyna (literally a song or folk song) is a traditional solo warm up—perfect for a prelude—typically played in the violin or clarinet. In that warm-up, the characteristics of Klezmer modes that convey those centuries of pain and longing are explored (and may also demonstrate the soloist’s virtuosity). The defining feature of that emotional expression is in the krekhts (literally, cracks): grace notes and ornamentations, breaks in tone, sobs and sighs, the catching of breaths in the middle of sobs (for more on why I write “the defining feature,” see Klezmer Modes and Dances, an Explainer in tomorrow’s blogpost).

Capturing the essence of krekhts on the piano is difficult. Some of it comes from the piano preparations: to try to evoke the sound of an Eastern European cimbalom or other sorts of zithers, I placed paper on the strings, and on top of the paper I placed snare drum snares—the bands of light metal chains that rest against the bottom head of a snare drum. This adds a buzzy sound, and restrains the sound from just singing out—there is something (emotional?) holding it back. (The music can also be performed without the preparations.) But I also have the pianist press against one or another of the strings, to choke off the sound from time to time.

A doyna is typically followed by a more upbeat dance. Here, it is followed by a Terkisher Tanz (Turkish Dance; often referred to simply as a Terkisher). This style of dance features three unequal steps per measure, two long and one short, producing a 3+3+2 meter (this can be heard in the countermelodies to the fugue subject). Adding to this rhythmic lumpiness, the first beat of a Terkisher is traditionally stretched out. Just like a traditional Terkisher, there is also a contrasting section, with a more energetic melody in a “happier” key.

But this is a fugue (with four voices)—in fact, the contrasting theme gets treated fugally as well, so this is a double fugue (see Single, Double and Triple Fugues: an Explainer, August 2, 2025)! There is something about this sort of juxtaposition of two completely different musical cultures that I just love. The music immerses itself deeply enough that it respects both cultures, but superficially enough that it allows for tradition crossing. (Here, and with Prelude and Fugue No.12, the traditions are Klezmer and fugue; Nos. 1 and 5 cross Gamelan and fugue, and Nos. 2 and 10 blend aspects of Chinese musical traditions with fugue.) So Klezmer doesn’t usually have counterpoint—what if it did? So fugues are usually written in the major or the minor modes—what if it were written in the “Freygish” mode?

These pieces were loosely inspired by the paintings The Green Violinist (1923-1924) and Musicians (1979) by the Belarusian-born French artist Marc Chagall (1887-1985). The Violinist might play a doyna, while in Musicians a bride and musicians celebrate her wedding. Michael Mizrahi does a great job tapping into the Jewish soul with his performances of these pieces, bringing out the sorrow and pain in the Prelude and the in the Fugue.
The defining feature of Klezmer is in the krekhts (or cracks): grace notes and ornamentations, breaks in tone, sobs and sighs, the catching of breaths in the middle of sobs.
